title: Aspiration event
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise acute respiratory compromise during feeding and activate the emergency response while stopping potentially unsafe feed delivery.
Do not use a tube again until its position is confirmed by the approved method.
Know that listening over the stomach is not a safe check.
Distinguish initial airway/oxygenation assessment from clinician-led diagnosis of aspiration, equipment rescue and decisions about restarting feed.

sources.use: NICE CG32 nasogastric tube position confirmation statements
NHS misplaced nasogastric tube patient safety alert
Indexed NHS enduring standards and previously mapped SK-11 safety principles; direct current page retrieval limited.

required_sources: Aspiration management guideline (airway clearing, suction, radiology) read in full
Unit enteral feeding and tube-position policy
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
First-line airway management after aspiration is not drawn from a source read and is not written.
The approved position check differs by country and product; the scenario names no pH threshold.

Case does not teach suctioning, positive-pressure rescue, intubation, bronchoscopy, antibiotic decisions or a validated diagnostic pathway for aspiration; obtain current locally approved airway response and enteral-feeding incident policy.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
setting: A fictional adult receiving enteral feed through a nasogastric tube on a fictional unit.

steps.info: Soon after a feed starts the patient coughs, becomes breathless and the saturation falls.

options.text: Stop the feed immediately, remain with the patient, assess airway, breathing and oxygenation, and urgently call the responsible emergency/critical-care team for new respiratory distress. Follow the approved airway/oxygen escalation plan with a competent clinician while the tube remains out of use.
options.feedback: Acute coughing, increased work of breathing and a falling saturation during feeding require prompt airway/respiratory assessment and urgent help while the feed is stopped. Misplaced-tube guidance supports withholding use until reassessment, but it does not by itself establish an aspiration diagnosis or prescribe rescue ventilation, suction or positioning for every patient.
options.consequence: The feed stops and urgent respiratory help is requested while the patient is assessed and supported under local protocol.

options.text: Slow the feed and watch for a while.
options.feedback: Continuing the feed after respiratory distress risks more harm.
options.consequence: The patient's breathing worsens as feed continues.

options.text: Flush the tube to clear it and carry on.
options.feedback: Introducing fluid into a tube of uncertain position risks harm.

steps.info: The team is at the bedside and asks whether the tube can be used.

options.text: Keep feed, water, medicines and flushes through the suspect tube withheld until position is confirmed by the approved method and documented by trained staff, and the team authorises use. Arrange essential medicines by an authorised alternative route if needed.
options.feedback: Prior checks or unchanged external markers do not guarantee current safe tube position. Approved tests and documented interpretation are required; resolution of respiratory symptoms alone is not permission to restart the feed. Do not use a trial flush or the appearance of aspirate alone to resolve uncertainty. If aspiration or pH assessment is inconclusive, seek the approved alternative confirmation pathway. The team must also reassess aspiration risk and ongoing respiratory status before feeding resumes.
options.consequence: The tube position is checked properly and the plan is agreed.

options.text: Restart the feed because the position was checked yesterday.
options.feedback: Position is confirmed before each use according to the policy, not carried over from an earlier check.
options.consequence: The feed restarts through a tube that may be misplaced.

options.text: Confirm the position by listening over the stomach while air is injected.
options.feedback: NHS England's enduring standards reject auscultation as a position-confirmation method; an unchanged external mark or aspirate appearance alone is also insufficient.
options.consequence: A misplaced tube is wrongly accepted.

steps.info: The patient is stable and the charge nurse asks for a report.

options.text: Document the timeline of feed delivery, respiratory symptoms, observations, verification method, actions and team response. Give a structured handover and report suspected tube misplacement or aspiration through the hospital safety pathway.
options.feedback: Precise documentation enables the clinical team to assess the event and determine whether it meets the local incident-reporting criteria. A possible aspiration is not automatically proof the tube was misplaced.
options.consequence: The review includes how the position was checked.

options.text: Record only that the patient coughed.
options.feedback: An incomplete record loses the timing and the checks.
options.consequence: The review cannot reconstruct what happened.

options.text: Say nothing, as the patient recovered.
options.feedback: Events are reported so that they can be learned from.

learning_points: New respiratory distress during feeding requires stopping the feed, immediate patient-first airway and oxygenation assessment and urgent emergency-team escalation.

Withhold all tube use, including flushes, water and medicines, while position is uncertain. Confirm with the approved method and documented interpretation before restarting; never use the whoosh test.
A respiratory event during feeding may have several causes; tube position and aspiration require qualified assessment, not an automatic diagnosis from coughing or a single saturation reading.
